title: Glial Cells
intro: Glia are the non-neuronal cells of the nervous system: astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and their relatives. They are roughly as numerous as neurons in the human brain (the old claim of ten glia per neuron is wrong; the ratio is close to one overall; Azevedo et al. 2009; von Bartheld et al. 2016). They do not fire action potentials, but they shape what neurons compute: astrocytes regulate synapses and respond to activity with calcium signals, oligodendrocytes set conduction speed, and microglia prune synapses. Most spiking network models leave them out, and that is usually a defensible simplification, but there are well-developed models of each.

items: Structure: star-shaped cells whose fine processes contact blood vessels and wrap synapses. In rodent hippocampus one astrocyte's non-overlapping domain holds an estimated 140,000 synapses (Bushong et al. 2002); human astrocytes are larger and more complex (Oberheim et al. 2009). Astrocytes are coupled to each other by gap junctions into networks.

Housekeeping that matters for computation: they clear glutamate from synapses through transporters (shaping synaptic time course and limiting spillover), buffer extracellular potassium, supply lactate to neurons and control local blood flow.

Calcium signalling: neurotransmitter acting on astrocytic G-protein receptors raises IP3, releasing calcium from internal stores. The resulting calcium transients and waves last seconds and spread within and between astrocytes.

The tripartite synapse: Araque et al. (1999) proposed that a synapse consists of presynaptic terminal, postsynaptic site and the astrocyte process around them, and that astrocytes respond to transmitter and release 'gliotransmitters' (glutamate, ATP/adenosine, D-serine) that modulate synaptic strength. Whether astrocytes release glutamate in a vesicular, neuron-like way in vivo is contested (Fiacco & McCarthy 2018; Savtchouk & Volterra 2018), but their role in neuromodulation is better supported: in mice and zebrafish, noradrenaline acts through astrocyte calcium to change network state (Paukert et al. 2014; Mu et al. 2019).

blocks.text: Oligodendrocytes wrap axons in the central nervous system with myelin, raising conduction velocity five- to fifty-fold through saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier. One oligodendrocyte can myelinate up to around 50 axon segments. Myelination is plastic: it changes with learning and activity in adults (McKenzie et al. 2014; Gibson et al. 2014), which could tune conduction delays. For a spiking model, this is the biological basis for learnable synaptic delays, which some SNN training methods now exploit (for example delay learning in Hammouamri, Khalfaoui-Hassani & Masquelier 2024).

Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells. Their processes constantly survey the tissue (Nimmerjahn, Kirchhoff & Helmchen 2005), and they remove synapses tagged by complement proteins during development, a form of activity-dependent pruning (Schafer et al. 2012). They also respond to injury and are implicated in many diseases. In modelling terms, pruning by microglia is one biological counterpart to structural plasticity: removing weak or unused synapses.

items: Li and Rinzel (1994): a two-variable reduction of the De Young-Keizer (1992) IP3 receptor model, describing calcium release from internal stores with an IP3-dependent oscillation. It is the core of nearly every astrocyte calcium model.
De Pitta et al. (2009): the 'G-ChI' model adding IP3 production and degradation to Li-Rinzel, reproducing amplitude- and frequency-modulated calcium oscillations driven by glutamate.

Tripartite synapse models: Nadkarni and Jung (2003) coupled a Li-Rinzel astrocyte to a Hodgkin-Huxley neuron; Volman, Ben-Jacob and Levine (2007) modelled astrocytic regulation of short-term synaptic plasticity; De Pitta, Volman, Berry and Ben-Jacob (2011) showed astrocytes could switch synapses between depressing and facilitating.

Network models: the review by Manninen, Havela and Linne (2018) surveys dozens of astrocyte and neuron-astrocyte models; Stimberg et al. (2019) provide Brian2 implementations of many of them for large networks.
Myelin and delays: cable models of myelinated axons (McIntyre, Richardson & Grill 2002) and SNN models with plastic delays.
Machine learning analogy: Kozachkov, Kastanenka and Krotov (2023) argued that neuron-astrocyte networks can implement transformer-like attention, a speculative but concrete proposal.

blocks.source:
Li-Rinzel (1994) astrocyte calcium, per unit cytosol volume

dC/dt = J_chan + J_leak - J_pump
J_chan = r_C · m∞³ · n∞³ · h³ · (C_ER - C)     IP3R channel release
   m∞  = IP3 / (IP3 + d1)                       IP3 activation
   n∞  = C / (C + d5)                           Ca activation
J_pump = v_ER · C² / (C² + K_ER²)                SERCA re-uptake
dh/dt  = (h∞ - h) / τ_h                          slow Ca inactivation
   h∞  = Q2 / (Q2 + C),  τ_h = 1 / (a2 (Q2 + C)),  Q2 = d2 (IP3 + d1)/(IP3 + d3)

At intermediate IP3, C oscillates on a timescale of seconds.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: Leaving glia out is the norm and usually fine for a first column model.

The glial functions most worth copying are cheap: slow, local modulation of synaptic strength (an astrocyte-like variable integrating activity over seconds), learnable delays (myelin), and pruning of weak synapses (microglia).

If you model astrocytes explicitly, use Li-Rinzel calcium dynamics driven by local synaptic activity and let the calcium scale release probability or add a slow current; the Brian2 implementations of Stimberg et al. (2019) are a good starting point.
